blocks.title: Script: six signs and two marks

segments.text: Six vowel signs, cold. Each attaches to a consonant and replaces the a built into it:

The last is the odd one. ೃ writes a vowel that behaves like a consonant in the mouth, inherited from Sanskrit and rare enough that a reader can go pages without meeting it — which is exactly why it is here.
Two marks now, and they are not vowel signs at all.

segments.instruction: ೊ and ೋ back to back, and say what separates them

segments.text: ಂ and ಃ ride after a syllable rather than reshaping its vowel. That is the division worth keeping: a vowel sign changes the sound already there, a mark adds one behind it.
Which of the eight writes a vowel that acts like a consonant? (ೃ.) Which two follow a syllable instead of reshaping it? (ಂ and ಃ.) And which one only makes the vowel longer? (ಾ.)

segments.text: Two full-size letters, not signs. Name the one that says i and the one that says u.

blocks.title: Script: the same vowel, two shapes

utterances: standing letter: ಇ. sound: i. when you use it: the word opens on the vowel.
standing letter: ಈ. sound: ī. when you use it: the same, held long.
standing letter: ಉ. sound: u. when you use it: the word opens on the vowel.
standing letter: ಊ. sound: ū. when you use it: the same, held long.
standing letter: ಓ. sound: ō. when you use it: the word opens on the vowel.

segments.text: Every one of these has a partner among the signs. The difference is not the sound — it is whether a consonant is there to carry it. A vowel with nothing in front of it must be written full-size; the moment a consonant arrives, the same vowel shrinks to a sign hanging off it.
Two pairs make this visible: ಇ against ಿ, and ಓ against ೋ. Same vowel, twice, and the shape tells you where in the word you are.

blocks.title: Script: ten, sorted by where they are made

segments.text: These ten arrived one per chapter, scattered from the book's opening to well past its middle, and no page ever put them side by side. Sorted by the mouth rather than by the order you met them:

utterances: where: throat. letters: ಕ ka, ಗ ga.
where: palate. letters: ಚ ca, ಝ jha, ಞ ña.

segments.text: Read down the middle row. ಚ, ಝ and ಞ are made in the same place, and they differ only in voice, breath and nasality — which is the organising idea the whole Kannada consonant grid is built on.
ಞ is the one to look at twice. It is the nasal of the palatal row and is rare on the page; a reader who has not seen it since the chapter that taught it will not place it at all.
Three that belong to no stop row, and one more from above.
